title: Table Scan vs. Index Seek
description: An equality lookup on an unindexed column scans the whole table; a nonclustered index turns the Clustered Index Scan into a fast Index Seek. Why it matters: this is the single most common cause of a "why is the app suddenly slow" ticket -- and usually a five-minute fix once you know what to check.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About
This lesson is about the single most common performance problem in any database: asking for a few rows but making the engine look at *all* of them. You'll see the difference between a **table scan** (checking every row, one by one) and an **index seek** (jumping straight to the rows you need).

Why does this happen? A table on its own is just a big pile of rows with no particular fast way to find "the ones where CustomerId = 42." Unless you build a helper structure, the database has no shortcut — it has to open every page and check every row itself.

Here's the mental model: think of a huge phone book with no alphabetical order — names just written down in the order people signed up. If you want everyone named "Smith," you have to read every single page, front to back. That's a table scan.

Now imagine someone re-sorts a copy of that phone book by last name and tapes labels on it. Suddenly you can flip straight to the "S" section. That's what an **index** does — it's a separate, sorted copy of some columns that lets SQL Server jump straight to the matching rows instead of reading everything. This lesson shows you how to spot the "reading everything" problem in a query plan, and how adding the right index turns a slow scan into a fast, targeted seek.

## Scenario
An order-lookup screen runs `SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE CustomerId = 42` on a 200,000-row table. It feels sluggish and gets worse as the table grows.

## Why it's slow
`Orders` has a clustered primary key on `OrderId`, but **nothing** supports the `CustomerId` predicate. SQL Server must read *every* page of the table and check each row — a **Clustered Index Scan**. Cost and logical reads grow linearly with table size.

## What to look for
- In the plan: a **Clustered Index Scan** on `Orders` reading ~all rows.
- In `STATISTICS IO`: **logical reads** in the hundreds+ for a query returning ~40 rows.
- A green **Missing Index** hint from the optimizer.

## The concept
An index whose key matches the search predicate lets SQL Server **seek** directly to the matching rows instead of scanning the whole table. The fix is a nonclustered index on `CustomerId`.
hints: Look at the operator reading Orders — is it a Scan or a Seek? A Scan touches every page.
There is no index whose key column is CustomerId, so the predicate can't be seeked.
Create a nonclustered index: CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Orders_CustomerId ON Orders(CustomerId);
